newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: South Asia report urges cuts in military spending.
newsitem.headline: South Asia report urges cuts in military spending.

text.p: South Asia should slash military spendings to finance basic social services like education, healthcare and supply of safe drinking water, said an annual human development report launched in Dhaka on Saturday.

"If military spending is cut, for instance, by five percent a year in real terms, it can generate a peace dividend of around $8.0 billion a year and can finance most of the basic social services package," said the report, written by Dr. Mahbubul Haq, Pakistan's former finance and planning minister.

"If South Asian countries display the required statemenship and vision and if they find a peaceful solution to their outstanding disputes, they can radically transform the development prospects of the region," the report said.

Haq said leaders of the member countries of South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) should agree to cut defence spending in line with the rest of the world and earmark resources for urgent social priority needs.
"It's time in the life of our nations when they should overcome the bitter legacy of the past and cultivate a new harvest of hope," he said.

The report proposed a 15-year plan of action for SAARC countries to help them to provide universal primary education, basic healthcare and safe drinking water for all, adequate nutrition for malnourished children, family planning services for at least 80 percent of married couples, and access to credit facilities for the poor and the deprived.
SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

A.M.A. Muhit, Bangladesh's former finance minister who attended the launch of the report, said: "Bangladesh has the highest expenditure in the defence sector which is 1.5 percent of the gross domestic products."
He urged the country's leaders to divert the "lion's share" of fundings to social development.

The World Bank's Dhaka mission chief, Pierre Landell-Mills, said: "If the military expenditure of Bangladesh can be diverted to the human resource sector, the country can go one step forward in achieving the target of GDP growth."
Bangladesh expects to raise GDP growth to 7 percent by year 2000 from the present 5.5 percent, officials said.
Finance Minister S.M.A.S. Kibria said: "We must have high growth with stress on social development."

Khadija Haq, the executive vice-president of the Human Development Centre in Islamabad, said: "Lacking other natural resources and threatened by ecological degradation, the main resource of Bangladesh was its people.
"The country can make rapid progress if it invests liberally in this resource."
She said Bangladesh spends only $5 (five) a year per person on providing education and health services. "This is very low compared to an investment of $10 in Pakistan and $14 in India."
The report lauded some achievements in Bangladesh like the immunisation of children against diseases and women's participation in economic activity.
"Immunisation coverage in Bangladesh is the highest in South Asia, having risen dramatically from less than one per cent in 1981 to over 80 percent by 1990," the report said.
